newsitem.title: GERMANY: German mkts watchdog tallies 1996 insider toll.
newsitem.headline: German mkts watchdog tallies 1996 insider toll.

text.p: Germany's efforts to stamp out financial market abuses and improve investor protection came to the fore on Tuesday, as its increasingly active stock market regulator tallied its achievements in 1996.

The Frankfurt-based Federal Supervisory Authority for Securities Trading, or BAWe, said that in 1996, its second year of operation, it passed on seventeen cases of suspected insider trading to public prosecutors compared with seven in 1995.

"The tasks of the BAWe will be increasing over the next few years," the agency's report said. "The experience gained during the first two years of operation has shown the positive effects of the regulatory system."

Insider deals were criminalised for the first time in Germany in mid-1994 as part of a package of reforms -- widely viewed as long overdue -- intended to bring the country's investor protection measures up to international standards.
The BAWe, the linchpin of Germany's drive to put a stop to insider trading, was equipped in 1996 with an electronic share trading surveillance system that processed 80 million trading reports.
In its annual report, the agency said four insider cases led to convictions last year, all incurring heavy fines.
A network of co-operation agreements with other market watchdogs enabled the agency to address 41 enquiries on insider deals to foreign authorities.
The BAWe also upped its efforts to clamp down on other aspects of investment services, such as monitoring banks' compliance with rules on investor safeguards and transparency.

For the first time, it collected centrally prospectuses for securities not listed on the stock exchange but offered to the public. The BAWe also attempted to force non-regulated investment firms on the "grey" capital market to comply with rules governing regulated firms.
The BAWe's powers are to be extended to give it jurisdiction over this unregulated market segment as soon as the definition of an investment services firm is broadened under Europe-wide laws.

Looking ahead, the BAWe said it would investigate the use of new media, such as the Internet, to make information on altered corporate voting rights, for example, more rapidly accessible to the public.

More broadly, the BAWe will be focusing on the next generation of German markets legislation in the form of the Third Financial Promotion Act, a set of laws designed to deregulate and modernise the legal framework.
